doctrines/mission-religions/question: What is the Church sent to do, and how does Christ relate to the world’s religions?
doctrines/mission-religions/summary: From the Great Commission and Justin’s "seeds of the Word" to Jesuit accommodation and the Chinese Rites, the Protestant missionary movement, the three-self principle, Vatican II, Lausanne and the southward shift of Christianity, this section traces debates over mission, culture, colonialism, religious liberty and the salvation of non-Christians.
doctrines/mission-religions/longText:
The risen Christ sent his followers to make disciples of all nations, and within three centuries the faith had spread from Ireland to India and Ethiopia. From the start Christians held two convictions in tension. One was that there is "none other name" by which people are saved. The other was that God had "not left himself without witness" among the nations. Justin Martyr saw seeds of the divine Word in Socrates. Cyprian taught that there is no salvation outside the Church, and the Council of Florence (1442) applied the maxim strictly. Missionary practice was just as varied. Gregory the Great told missionaries to convert pagan temples rather than destroy them. The Church of the East presented Christ in Buddhist and Daoist idiom in Tang China. Spanish conquest tied baptism to the sword, and Las Casas protested that faith can only be offered by persuasion.

In the 17th century the Jesuits Ricci and de Nobili adopted Chinese and Indian dress, language and thought. The Chinese Rites controversy ended with papal bans (1704–1742) that crippled the mission until they were reversed in 1939. William Carey (1792) launched the Protestant missionary movement, which planted churches across Asia, Africa and the Pacific, often in the shadow of empire. Henry Venn and John Nevius urged self-supporting, self-governing, self-propagating churches, but paternalism often blocked them, as in the treatment of Bishop Samuel Ajayi Crowther. The Edinburgh conference of 1910 dreamed of evangelising the world in a generation and gave birth to the ecumenical movement.

The 20th century reframed both mission and the religions. At Tambaram (1938) Kraemer argued that the gospel stands in discontinuity with all religions. Willingen (1952) grounded mission in the missio Dei, the sending of the triune God. Rahner proposed "anonymous Christians", Vatican II taught respect for what is "true and holy" in other faiths and affirmed religious freedom (Dignitatis Humanae, 1965), and John Hick called for a pluralist "Copernican revolution". Evangelicals at Lausanne (1974) reaffirmed Christ’s uniqueness and, prompted by Latin Americans, integral mission. They later divided between restrictivism and a "wider hope". Meanwhile Christianity’s centre of gravity moved to the Global South. Andrew Walls and Lamin Sanneh argued that the translatable gospel had escaped its colonial carriers, and missionaries now go out from Seoul, Lagos and São Paulo. Each position is presented here in its own terms, with its strongest critics.
doctrines/mission-religions/flow/nodes/0: What is the Church sent to do, and how does Christ relate to the world’s religions?

Jesus sent his disciples to "teach all nations", and the apostles proclaimed that "there is none other name under heaven" by which we must be saved. Yet Paul told the Athenians that God "left not himself without witness". Must people hear of Christ to be saved? How should missionaries treat other cultures and religions? Was modern mission the servant of empire or the seed of world Christianity?
doctrines/mission-religions/flow/nodes/1: The Great Commission (Matt 28:18–20; Luke 24:47; Acts 1:8)

"Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them ... teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you." The risen Christ sends his witnesses "unto the uttermost part of the earth".
doctrines/mission-religions/flow/nodes/2: "None other name" (John 14:6; Acts 4:12; 1 Tim 2:5)

"No man cometh unto the Father, but by me"; "neither is there salvation in any other"; "one mediator between God and men". Exclusivists read these as requiring explicit faith; inclusivists as saying that all who are saved are saved by Christ.
doctrines/mission-religions/flow/nodes/3: God’s witness among the nations (Acts 14:17; 17:22–31; Rom 1:19–20; 2:14–16)

At Lystra and Athens Paul speaks of the God who "left not himself without witness", quotes pagan poets and finds an altar "to the unknown god"; Romans speaks of creation’s testimony and a law written on Gentile hearts, yet also of humanity "without excuse".
doctrines/mission-religions/flow/nodes/4: Every nation, tribe and tongue (Gen 12:3; Rev 7:9; 21:24–26)

God’s promise that in Abraham "all families of the earth" will be blessed ends in a multitude from "all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues" and the glory of the nations brought into the New Jerusalem.
doctrines/mission-religions/flow/nodes/5: Justin: seeds of the Word among the Greeks (c.155)

Justin holds that the divine Logos sowed seeds of truth in every people, so that Socrates and others who lived by reason were in a sense Christians before Christ: an early source for inclusivist thought.
doctrines/mission-religions/flow/nodes/6: Cyprian: no salvation outside the Church (c.256)
In the rebaptism dispute Cyprian insists that grace and salvation are found only within the one Church; the maxim extra ecclesiam nulla salus becomes a pillar of later teaching.
doctrines/mission-religions/flow/nodes/7: Gregory the Great: convert the temples, not destroy them (601)

Writing to the mission to the English, Gregory advises that pagan temples be purified and reused and festivals turned to Christian feasts, because people rise "by degrees": a classic text of missionary adaptation.
doctrines/mission-religions/flow/nodes/8: The Church of the East in Tang China (635–781)

East Syriac missionaries from Persia reach Chang’an (635); the Xi’an Stele (781) presents the "Luminous Religion" in Buddhist and Daoist vocabulary. Their creative translation has been praised as early inculturation and criticised as syncretism.
doctrines/mission-religions/flow/nodes/9: Restrictivism: explicit faith and membership required (Florence, 1442)

The Council of Florence’s decree for the Copts (Cantate Domino, 1442) declares that pagans, Jews, heretics and schismatics outside the Catholic Church cannot share eternal life unless joined to it before death. Many Protestants likewise held that only those who hear and believe the gospel are saved.
doctrines/mission-religions/flow/nodes/1: Conquest and conversion in the Americas (1492–1550)

The papal bulls of 1493 and the Spanish Requerimiento (1513), read to Indigenous peoples before attack, tie evangelisation to conquest; mass baptisms follow violence, enslavement and epidemic. Franciscans, Dominicans and Jesuits also build schools, hospitals and Indigenous-language literature.
Las Casas: the gospel must be offered by persuasion, not force (1537–1550)

Bartolomé de las Casas argues (The Only Way, c.1537) that faith must be freely embraced, and at Valladolid (1550–51) defends Indigenous rights against Sepúlveda’s case for just war and "natural slavery".
Jesuit accommodation: Ricci and de Nobili (1601–1610)

Matteo Ricci adopts the dress of a Confucian scholar, uses the classics to speak of the "Lord of Heaven", and treats ancestor and Confucius rites as civil honours; Roberto de Nobili lives as a Brahmin ascetic in Madurai.
Rome bans the Chinese Rites (1704–1742)

After protests by Dominicans and Franciscans, Clement XI condemns the rites (1704; Ex illa die, 1715) and Benedict XIV’s Ex quo singulari (1742) ends debate. The Kangxi Emperor responds by restricting the mission. Pius XII reverses the ban in 1939.
William Carey and the Protestant missionary movement (1792)
Carey’s Enquiry and the Baptist Missionary Society launch a wave of voluntary societies (LMS 1795, CMS 1799, ABCFM 1810); Carey’s Serampore team translates the Bible into dozens of Indian languages.
The indigenous principle: self-supporting, self-governing, self-propagating (1850s–1890)

Henry Venn (CMS) and Rufus Anderson (ABCFM) set the goal of "three-self" churches; John Nevius’s plan (1886, adopted in Korea from 1890) and Roland Allen’s Missionary Methods (1912) press local leadership from the start.
Samuel Ajayi Crowther, first African Anglican bishop (1864)

A rescued Yoruba slave, Crowther is consecrated bishop of the Niger (1864), the fruit of Venn’s policy; in the 1880s younger European missionaries undermine his mission, and he is succeeded by a European, a turning point in African disillusionment with missionary paternalism.
Mission and empire: the high imperial age (1880–1914)

The Berlin Conference (1884–85) partitions Africa; missions often rely on colonial protection and share racial assumptions. Critics from Gandhi to postcolonial historians portray mission as cultural imperialism; others show missionaries opposing slavery, forced labour and settler abuses.
Edinburgh World Missionary Conference (1910)

Some 1,200 delegates (only about 20 from Asia and none from Africa) plan the "evangelization of the world in this generation" under John R. Mott; the conference births the International Missionary Council (1921) and the ecumenical movement.
Particularism: Kraemer at Tambaram (1938)

At the IMC meeting in Tambaram, India, Hendrik Kraemer, influenced by Barth, argues for the "discontinuity" of the gospel with all religions; Indian Christians such as P. Chenchiah protest that this ignores God’s work in Indian religious life.
doctrines/mission-religions/flow/nodes/2: Rome rejects strict extra ecclesiam (1949)
The Holy Office letter on Leonard Feeney teaches that those invincibly ignorant of the Church may be saved by an implicit desire informed by charity, opening the way to Vatican II’s inclusivism.
Missio Dei: mission belongs to God (Willingen, 1952)

After the expulsion of missionaries from China, the IMC at Willingen roots mission in the Trinity: the Father sends the Son, the Father and Son send the Spirit, and the triune God sends the Church. Later ecumenical versions stress God’s work in history and "humanisation".
China’s Three-Self Patriotic Movement (1954)

The communist state adopts the three-self language to cut churches off from foreign missions under party oversight; unregistered house churches resist. Ironically, Chinese Protestantism grows from under one million (1949) to tens of millions without missionaries.
Inclusivism: "anonymous Christians" (Rahner, 1961)
Karl Rahner argues that God’s universal saving will means grace is offered to all, including through other religions; those who accept it are saved by Christ as "anonymous Christians".
Vatican II on the religions and mission (1964–65)

Lumen Gentium 16 says those who without fault do not know Christ but seek God sincerely may attain salvation; Nostra Aetate (1965) says the Church rejects nothing true and holy in other religions; Ad Gentes reaffirms the missionary nature of the Church.
Religious liberty: Dignitatis Humanae (1965)

The Council affirms freedom from coercion in religion as a right grounded in human dignity: a principle long defended by Anabaptists, Baptists (Thomas Helwys, Roger Williams) and Quakers, now embraced by the Catholic Church and the WCC.
Pluralism: Hick’s "Copernican revolution" (1973)

John Hick proposes that the world religions are equally valid responses to one ultimate Reality; Paul Knitter, Wilfred Cantwell Smith and Stanley Samartha develop pluralist and liberationist versions.
Lausanne Covenant and integral mission (1974)

Evangelicals at Lausanne affirm the uniqueness of Christ and urgency of evangelism against universalism and pluralism, while Latin Americans René Padilla and Samuel Escobar win recognition of social responsibility; "integral mission" and "unreached people groups" (Ralph Winter) both emerge.
Contextualisation and inculturation (1972–1979)

Shoki Coe coins "contextualisation" (1972); Paul VI’s Evangelii Nuntiandi (1975) and Pedro Arrupe (1978) speak of evangelising cultures and "inculturation"; African theologians (John Mbiti, Kwame Bediako) and Asian theologians recover pre-Christian religious heritage as preparation for the gospel.
Translatability and world Christianity (Sanneh, Walls, 1989)

Lamin Sanneh and Andrew Walls argue that Bible translation made Christianity endlessly culturally translatable, so missions sowed vernacular renewal that escaped Western control; Robert Woodberry’s data (2012) link Protestant missions with literacy and democracy.
doctrines/mission-religions/flow/nodes/3: Clark Pinnock and John Sanders argue that the unevangelised may be saved by responding to the light they have; others propose post-mortem encounter with Christ. Ronald Nash and most confessional evangelicals defend restrictivism.

The Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith rejects pluralist theologies, affirms Christ as unique and universal saviour and the necessity of the Church, and investigates Jacques Dupuis’s inclusive pluralism (notified 2001).

By 2000 most Christians live in Africa, Asia and Latin America; Africa becomes the largest Christian continent by the 2010s. Walls, Sanneh, Philip Jenkins (The Next Christendom, 2002) and others describe "world Christianity" and "reverse mission" from South to North.

Catholic teaching combines Christ’s unique mediation with Vatican II inclusivism and dialogue; Orthodox churches stress the Church as ark of salvation while leaving judgement of others to God; most evangelicals and Pentecostals hold particularism, divided between restrictivism and wider-hope views; liberal Protestants often embrace pluralism. Mission now flows from everywhere to everywhere: Korea, Brazil and Nigeria send thousands of missionaries, while debates over proselytism, conversion laws (e.g. in India) and religious liberty intensify.
